title: The smaller emptiness
hookLine: the hall is empty of elephants and cattle, but not of monks: emptiness step by step

lines: THE BUDDHA POINTS AT THE BUILDING.
cards: Emptiness. It sounds like a void, a hollow feeling, maybe something sad. The hundred and twenty-first discourse starts with Ananda checking his memory.
Lord, he says, once among the Sakyans I think I heard you say: Ananda, I often dwell in emptiness. Did I hear that right? Yes, the Buddha says.
Then and now. And instead of describing a void, he points at the building they're sitting in.

teach.h: EMPTY OF ELEPHANTS, NOT OF MONKS
teach.b: This hall, Migara's mother's palace, the Buddha says, is empty of elephants, cattle and horses. Empty of gold and silver. Empty of crowds of men and women.
But it isn't empty of one thing: the community of monks. That's the whole idea in one picture. Emptiness, suññata, in this teaching is always empty of something.
You notice what isn't there, and you honestly notice what is. Then he walks it inward. A monk stops attending to the village and to people, and attends only to the forest.

His mind settles there. He sees: the busyness that came with the village isn't here; there's only the quiet of the forest. Then he lets the forest go and attends to earth, just its flatness, like a hide stretched smooth.
Then space without limit. Consciousness without limit. Nothingness.
A state too subtle to call perception or not. A stillness with no sign to hold. And last, a mind freed from the taints.
At each step, the same honest check: this is absent; this is still present.
Even at the end, the Buddha says, what remains is this body, alive, with its six senses.
Emptiness here isn't pretending nothing exists. It's a careful inventory, a room cleared one thing at a time, each step lighter than the last.
Look back at the week: one by one, the true person, the sages' mountain, the great forty, the breath read whole, a full jar.
And now a hall, empty of elephants, full of monks.

how: Emptiness is taught across Buddhist schools in different ways; in the Theravada reading of MN 121 it is a meditative descent, noticing at each stage what the mind is empty of and what remains, while Mahayana schools develop emptiness in their own way, in texts such as the Perfection of Wisdom sutras.

o: emptiness: seeing what something is empty of
a lonely, hollow feeling deep inside
a dark void where nothing at all exists

games.q: the smaller emptiness: tap the pairs.
p: what the hall isn't empty of
this living body, with its senses

s: in MN 121 emptiness means nothing exists at all
it's always empty of something: the hall is empty of cattle, but the monks are really there.
Ananda checks whether he remembered the Buddha's words correctly
he asks if he heard 'I often dwell in emptiness', and the Buddha says yes.
the steps go from forest to earth to boundless space
and on through consciousness and nothingness to a stillness without signs, and finally release.

games.q: you've let go of thoughts of the village and attend only to the forest. what does the monk in MN 121 notice?
o: the busyness of the village isn't here; only the forest's quiet is.
the forest is also full of crowds.
games.why: he sees honestly what's absent and what's present: no village busyness, only the quiet that comes with the forest.

practice: Look around: this room is empty of the ocean, of a crowd, maybe of noise, and not empty of a chair, light, your breathing.
Then close your eyes and do it inside: empty of yesterday's argument, empty of tomorrow's meeting, not empty of this breath.

wordCard.voice: Suññata. Emptiness as the Buddha teaches it here: seeing what something is empty of, and honestly what remains, step by step.

orig.note: Pali suññata: emptiness. Sanskrit shunyata. here, always empty of something.

carryVoice: Your line: empty of this. What's absent and what's here can both be seen. That's the week.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 121, Culasuññata Sutta (the smaller discourse on emptiness)
